title: Linked List Cycle II — find the start of the cycle.
shortTitle: Linked List Cycle II — Find the Start of the Cycle

s1_definition.profdef: Linked List Cycle II finds the node where a cycle begins, or reports none. It first uses Floyd's tortoise and hare to find a meeting point inside the loop, then resets one pointer to the head and advances both pointers one step at a time; the node where they meet again is the cycle's entry point. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India not only wants to know a transaction chain loops, but exactly which node the loop re-enters, so it can snip the bad link. Rajesh first catches the two fingers inside the loop, then moves one finger back to the start and walks both one step at a time; the spot where they meet again is where the loop begins.
s1_definition.oneliner: After the tortoise and hare meet, move one pointer to the head and step both by one; their next meeting is the cycle's start.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Linked List Cycle II finds the node where a cycle begins, or reports none. It first uses Floyd's tortoise and hare to find a meeting point inside the loop, then resets one pointer to the head and advances both pointers one step at a time; the node where they meet again is the cycle's entry point. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India not only wants to know a transaction chain loops, but exactly which node the loop re-enters, so it can snip the bad link. Rajesh first catches the two fingers inside the loop, then moves one finger back to the start and walks both one step at a time; the spot where they meet again is where the loop begins.

**One line to remember:** After the tortoise and hare meet, move one pointer to the head and step both by one; their next meeting is the cycle's start.

sections.s2_technical:
Phase one is ordinary Floyd detection: advance slow by one and fast by two until they meet, or return null if fast reaches the end. Phase two: set one pointer back to the head, keep the other at the meeting point, and advance both by one node per step. The node where they meet is the start of the cycle.

A code snippet: `Node detectCycleStart(Node head) { Node slow = head, fast = head; while (fast != null && fast.next != null) { slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next.next; if (slow == fast) { Node p = head; while (p != slow) { p = p.next; slow = slow.next; } return p; } } return null; }`. The second loop advances both by one until they coincide at the entry node.

The math behind phase two is the senior-level explanation. Let the distance from the head to the cycle start be `a`, and let the slow pointer have traveled `a + b` to the meeting point where `b` is the distance from the cycle start to the meeting point. Because fast travels twice as far, `2(a + b) = a + b + n*L` for some whole number of loops `L`, which simplifies to `a = n*L - b`. That means the distance from the head to the cycle start equals the distance from the meeting point onward to the cycle start (modulo full loops), so stepping both pointers one at a time from the head and the meeting point lands them together exactly at the entry.

A senior nuance is that this elegant equality is why no counting or extra storage is needed; it falls out of the two-to-one speed ratio. The alternative hash-set method also finds the start but uses linear extra space. Handling the no-cycle case by returning null when fast falls off the end is essential.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India detected that an imported transaction chain loops, and now the repair tool must find the exact node where the loop re-enters so it can break that single bad link and restore a proper list. This is exactly how Cycle II works — it pinpoints the cycle's start node.

Problem 2 — The repair runs in the same memory-constrained import path, so the constant-space two-phase pointer method is used rather than a visited-set.

The code shows a `ChainRepairTool` with `findCycleStart`, a demo on a corrupted chain, and the identified entry node.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: chain T1 to T5 where T5 points back to T3, so the cycle starts at T3 with `a` equal to 2 (head to T3) and a loop of length 3 (T3, T4, T5).

Step 1: Phase one. Slow and fast start at T1. Slow to T2, fast to T3. Slow to T3, fast to T5. Slow to T4, fast jumps T5 then T3 then T4, so fast to T4. Slow equals fast at T4, the meeting point inside the loop.

Step 2: Phase two begins. A new pointer `p` starts at the head T1 while slow stays at the meeting point T4. Both will now move one step at a time.

Step 3: `p` moves to T2 and slow moves from T4 to T5. They are different. `p` moves to T3 and slow moves from T5 back to T3.

Step 4: Now `p` equals slow at T3, which is exactly the node where the loop re-enters. The distance from the head to T3 was 2, and the distance from the meeting point around to T3 was also 2 steps, matching the formula.

Step 5: The tool returns T3 as the cycle start, so the repair code could then find the node whose next is T3 within the loop and null it to break the cycle.

```
2026-10-26 21:00:03 WARNING Cycle entry at T3
2026-10-26 21:00:03 INFO    Cycle starts at: T3
```
sections.s5b_flow:

    ▼
  Phase 2: p=head, slow=meeting

sections.s6_takeaway:
Linked List Cycle II finds the exact node where a cycle begins, and it builds on Floyd's tortoise and hare in two phases. In phase one I advance a slow pointer by one and a fast pointer by two until they meet inside the loop, or I return null if the fast pointer reaches the end. In phase two I move one pointer back to the head, keep the other at the meeting point, and advance both by a single node at a time; the node where they meet again is the start of the cycle.

The reason phase two works is a short piece of algebra I can walk through. If the distance from the head to the cycle start is a, and the slow pointer has traveled a plus b to reach the meeting point where b is the distance from the cycle start to the meeting point, then because the fast pointer traveled twice as far, two times a plus b equals a plus b plus some whole number of loop lengths. That simplifies to a equals a whole number of loop lengths minus b, which means the distance from the head to the entry equals the distance from the meeting point around to the entry. So stepping both pointers one at a time from those two places lands them together precisely at the cycle start.

That equality is exactly why no counting and no extra storage are needed; it falls straight out of the two-to-one speed ratio. The hash-set alternative also finds the start but uses linear extra space, and I always handle the acyclic case by returning null when the fast pointer runs off the end.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the chain repair tool. After detecting that an imported transaction chain looped, the tool needed the exact re-entry node so it could break that single bad link and restore a proper list, and because the repair ran in the same memory-constrained import path the constant-space two-phase method was ideal. Explaining the two phases, the distance equality that justifies the second phase, and the no-extra-memory property shows the interviewer I understand the mathematics behind this elegant algorithm.
